title: Where should the toy shop stop?
lead: The operator of Tokyo Skytree and a vending company want to try several places for one moving toy shop. They plan to watch where people stop and count what sells.

technology_signal.title: A toy shop can change places at the tower entrance
technology_signal.summary: At Tokyo Skytree, two companies have planned a trial for a toy shop that can move. They want to find out where more people stop to look and where more toys sell.
technology_signal.implications: To compare the different spots at Tokyo Skytree, the organizers plan to count the people who walk past the shop and those who stop.

news.title: A toy shop that can change places
news.summary: At the entrance to Tokyo Skytree, two companies planned an eight-day test for a toy shop that can move. They want to see where visitors stop and where they buy something.
news.details: One machine selling soft toys will move between locations on the Tokyo Skytree entrance floor.
news.technical_novelty: The organizers plan to change the selling spot and use a camera to estimate the share of passersby who stop.
news.engineering_impact: Counts of stops, purchases and survey responses give the tower operator different ways to evaluate a location.
news.limitations: The tower announcement describes the trial and gives no sales results.
news.evidence_status: The supplier and the operator of Tokyo Skytree announced the November 21–28 trial.
news.body:
Imagine heading to the ticket counter for a tower in Tokyo and spotting a little shop. The soft toys inside look like buns and pastries. The companies behind the test plan to move the machine around the entrance floor of Tokyo Skytree from November 21 to 28. They will watch what happens when the same shop is put in different places.

The sales record can tell them how many toys people bought. But visitors can stop to look and then walk on. The team plans to use a camera to find out what share of the people walking past actually stop. The companies also want to ask visitors what they thought of the shop.

A machine of this kind has operated at Narita Airport since April. The trial at the tower has its own surroundings, with many people heading for the ticket counters. The team will suggest taking a toy up to the viewing deck and photographing it with the city in the background. The companies have announced what they will measure, including how many people stop. The figures from the trial still have to be collected and reported.

news.title: A freight car that turns its own wheels
news.summary: Intramotev says a rail company plans to use its self-propelled freight cars at an industrial site in Texas. The cars have batteries and equipment that can drive their wheels along the track.
news.details: Watco plans to use Intramotev freight cars at an industrial site in Seadrift.
news.technical_novelty: A battery and drive system can move the freight car under its own power along the rails.
news.engineering_impact: For the assigned movement, the car can provide traction at its own wheels.
news.limitations: The partners' announcement gives no deployment size or starting date for the Texas site.
news.evidence_status: Manufacturer Intramotev reported the new agreement on November 20.
news.body:
A locomotive usually pulls or pushes a freight car when it needs to move. Intramotev makes a freight car that can turn its own wheels. On November 20 the company said a rail operator called Watco had agreed to use the cars at an industrial site in Seadrift, Texas.

Like a battery-powered toy car, this vehicle stores the electricity it needs to turn the wheels. Here the wheels have to carry a heavy load along rails. Once the car reaches the other end, someone still has to arrange for the load to come off and for the battery to be charged when needed.

The companies already made an agreement for a terminal in Illinois. Imagine a car making short trips there but waiting longer for its turn to load in Texas. Two identical cars could then carry different amounts of freight in a day. The company has yet to say how many cars will go to Seadrift or when they will begin moving freight there.

news.title: One arm picks a part, another guides a cable
news.summary: A Japanese company plans to take three robot arms to a show in Osaka. One will pick a metal part from a pile, one will repeat a movement shown by a person, and one will guide a cable around pins.
news.details: Exhibition setups in Osaka will use arms from FANUC, Universal Robots and Elite Robots.
news.technical_novelty: Chitose Robotics' software connects sensors and operator devices to industrial robot arms.
news.engineering_impact: In the metal picking demonstration, software uses the outline of a part to find a place for a suction cup.
news.limitations: The announcement gives no success rates or cycle times for the planned exhibition jobs.
news.evidence_status: Chitose Robotics announced the demonstrations in its exhibit preview.
news.body:
At a show in Osaka in early December, a company called Chitose Robotics plans to give three robot arms different jobs. One arm will lift a metal part out of a pile. Another will follow a path a person previously showed it. The third will lay a soft cable around several pins.

Imagine trying to pick something up with a suction cup. If the cup lands halfway off the edge, it might lose its grip. The first arm gets a camera that looks at the pile. A program uses the outline of the part in the image to decide where to put the cup and how to turn it.

The cable presents a different puzzle. The arm has to hold on to a flexible wire while it moves from pin to pin. A person gives the program a few points to follow, and the program fills in a smooth path between them. The announcement describes the work the company plans to show. It does not give a count of the parts an arm could pick in a whole shift, or say how long the cable job takes.

news.title: What if a pump starts to sound different?
news.summary: BrightAI announced $97 million to expand a system that watches industrial equipment. Sensors can listen to machines or measure how much they shake, so a computer nearby can pick up changes.
news.details: Smith Point Capital led the round, which also included GE Vernova.
news.technical_novelty: The BrightAI system analyses sensor readings on a computer close to the equipment.
news.engineering_impact: Local analysis can keep checking for changes when the connection to a remote server is interrupted.
news.limitations: The financing announcement gives no fault detection results for a specific site.
news.evidence_status: BrightAI announced the investment. Its lead investor described the system and its reported footprint.
news.body:
Picture a pump running in a room where nobody is around. Who would hear it if the sound changed? A US company called BrightAI makes equipment to help watch places like that. On November 18 it announced $97 million from investors, people and companies that pay to help a business grow.

Sensors sit near the machine. One can record sound, while another measures how much the machine shakes. A small computer nearby checks whether the latest readings look like the usual ones. It can do that work locally even when a link to a distant computer is interrupted. The lead investor also describes using robots or flying cameras to get a closer look when needed.

The investor says more than 50,000 places use the system. If a sensor gives a warning, someone still has to find out what changed. A worker could check whether the pump really has a fault. The funding announcement did not say how often these warnings caught faults before they got worse.

news.title: Who will make and support the factory robots?
news.summary: Reuters reported that Switzerland’s ABB was weighing other options for its industrial robot business. Chinese authorities have already barred Japan’s SoftBank from buying the part of that business in China.
news.details: Reuters reports discussions about separating ABB Robotics' Chinese business from the rest of the division.
news.technical_novelty: Reported alternatives include another buyer or a standalone company if the SoftBank sale falls through.
news.engineering_impact: The structure can matter to industrial customers that arrange parts and maintenance for robots.
news.limitations: The companies have not announced a final arrangement following the Reuters report.
news.evidence_status: ABB confirmed the restriction in China. The potential alternatives come from unnamed Reuters sources.
news.body:
Picture a factory where a robot lifts heavy parts. If the factory wants another robot or needs something repaired, it can contact the company that supplies the machine. Switzerland’s ABB agreed to sell its industrial robot business to SoftBank, a Japanese company. Now there is a question over who will own that business.

The robot business operates in several countries. ABB said Chinese authorities had barred SoftBank from buying the part in China. On November 20 Reuters reported that the companies were discussing ways to make the sale work. It talked to two people familiar with the discussions, whose names it kept private.

One option Reuters described would leave the Chinese operation outside the sale. If the deal falls through, the report says ABB could look for another buyer or make the robotics business a company of its own. Neither company has announced that it will take any of those steps. A factory planning its next order still has to wait to see who will sell and support its equipment.
